system: .NET: Roslyn front end, CoreCLR (RyuJIT, tiered compilation, OSR, Dynamic PGO, ReadyToRun/crossgen2, code versioning, the new CoreCLR interpreter), NativeAOT/ILC, and Mono (full AOT, interpreter, wasm AOT, jiterpreter). Sources read: dotnet/runtime clone at 0968772 (2026-11-18), dotnet/roslyn clone at 14798cd (2026-11-18), both local clones, plus Microsoft Learn pages and devblogs. The ep9 tree at m9-p5 (86e39c65) was read only to map the lessons onto its ADRs (H01, H05, H29, H32, H33, H35, H37, plan 13).

findings.claim: IL plus metadata is the one stable contract. Every executor reads it through one interface: the JIT, crossgen2 (R2R), ILC (NativeAOT) and the new CoreCLR interpreter. That interface is ICorJitInfo / ICorJitCompiler, about 184 methods, versioned by a single GUID.
findings.mechanism: The runtime (the EE) implements ICorJitInfo in C++ (vm/jitinterface.cpp). crossgen2 and ILC implement the same interface in C#, in one shared folder (tools/Common/JitInterface/CorInfoImpl.cs, 5,357 lines, plus CorInfoImpl.ReadyToRun.cs). The thunks are generated from ThunkInput.txt. Any change to the method list must bump JITEEVersionIdentifier, and ICorJitCompiler::getVersionIdentifier() checks it at load.
findings.numbers: ThunkInput.txt FUNCTIONS block: 184 entries; CorInfoImpl.cs 5,357 lines

findings.claim: RyuJIT is one binary for JIT, R2R and NativeAOT. The mode difference is a flag word plus an ABI query, not a fork. CORJIT_FLAG_AOT covers 'ReadyToRun or NativeAOT', and the NativeAOT-only differences are IsTargetAbi(CORINFO_NATIVEAOT_ABI) checks.
findings.mechanism: CORJIT_FLAGS bits pick the tier and mode: TIER0, TIER1, OSR, BBINSTR, BBINSTR_IF_LOOPS, BBOPT, AOT, RELOC, ASYNC and others. The EE side answers questions differently per mode. For example, crossgen2's CorInfoImpl.ReadyToRun.cs checks VersionsWithMethodBody before allowing an inline. In jit/*.cpp there are 49 IsTargetAbi(CORINFO_NATIVEAOT_ABI) sites and 13 IsReadyToRun() sites.
findings.numbers: 49 NativeAOT ABI checks, 13 IsReadyToRun checks in jit/*.cpp (grep at HEAD); 33+ CORJIT flag bits

findings.claim: The new CoreCLR interpreter plugs in as another ICorJitCompiler. Its compileMethod turns IL into interpreter bytecode, or returns CORJIT_SKIPPED, and then the runtime falls back to RyuJIT. It reuses the same JIT-EE interface, prestub and precode machinery.
findings.mechanism: The interpreter exports getJit(). The runtime tries the interpreter first (UnsafeJitFunction) and falls back to the EE JIT manager when the interpreter returns nothing. DOTNET_InterpMode has 4 modes. 0: off unless a method is listed. 1: everything except R2R code and CoreLib. 2: everything except intrinsics, and R2R is turned off. 3: interpreter only, with R2R off, HW intrinsics off and Vector<T> capped at 128 bits.
findings.numbers: InterpMode 0-3; interpreter source about 16,800 lines (src/coreclr/interpreter *.cpp/*.h)

findings.claim: At HEAD (2026-11), turning on the CoreCLR interpreter turns off tiered compilation. The code says 'Tiered compilation and interpreter do not work well together currently.' The interpreter tier was added after the tiering design and is not yet part of the tier ladder.
findings.mechanism: In eeconfig.cpp, if DOTNET_Interpreter or InterpMode != 0, fTieredCompilation = false. The 2018 tiering doc described an older IL interpreter that did use tiering to promote to jitted code. That interpreter was off by default.

findings.claim: Tier0 code is promoted after 30 calls, but counting starts only after a 100 ms startup delay. Any new Tier0 jitting during the delay restarts it. In debug builds the values are 2 calls and 1 ms, so more paths get exercised.
findings.mechanism: HandleCallCountingForFirstCall puts methods first called during the delay into m_methodsPendingCountingForTier1 instead of counting them, and sets a 'recently recorded' flag that extends the delay. The background worker sleeps delayMs in a loop until TryDeactivateTieringDelay finds no new methods, then installs call counters for all pending methods. On a single CPU the delay is multiplied by 10. The 2018 doc says 30 was picked with 'a small amount of early empirical testing', that +-5 'can vanish into the noise', and that a 10x change makes a notable difference.
findings.numbers: TC_CallCountThreshold=30, TC_CallCountingDelayMs=100, TC_DelaySingleProcMultiplier=10, debug 2/1 ms/2, background worker idle timeout 4,000 ms

findings.claim: In 2.1 the 100 ms timer ran once at startup and never restarted. The design doc lists that as a known issue: servers go idle and later 'jit heavily once again'. The current knob text calls the delay 'perpetual … while there is startup-like activity': it re-arms on any new burst of Tier0 activity.
findings.mechanism: The delay is active while m_methodsPendingCountingForTier1 != null. Each new first-call during a burst re-creates or extends it. Call counting that has already started is not stopped when the delay re-arms, because stopping and restarting costs more than finishing the count (callcounting.h summary).

findings.claim: Call counting moved from the prestub, which the 2018 doc called 'utterly naive' with a 'high per-invocation cost', to small per-method stubs. Each stub decrements a UINT16 cell, jumps to the code, and calls a helper at zero. The stubs are deleted in bulk once promotion is done.
findings.mechanism: CallCountingStub is 24 B of code on x64 (short and long forms) and 40 B on arm64. Methods without a precode (virtual methods with slot backpatching) get a forwarder precode, so the stub can be deleted safely. Hitting the threshold queues completion to the background thread. Cleanup suspends the runtime and deletes all stubs.
findings.numbers: stub code 24 B x64/x86, 40 B arm64/riscv64/loongarch64, 32 B arm32; count type UINT16

findings.claim: Tier1 work runs on one background worker. Its work slice adapts: it starts at (CPU count) ms, is capped at 50 ms, and grows to 1/4 of the measured time it was descheduled. The 2018 doc described a fixed 10 ms chunk.
findings.mechanism: After each slice the worker calls sleep(0) and measures how long it was away. The next slice is max(measured/4, decayed previous), clamped between min and max. The aim: don't monopolize CPU during startup, and don't yield so often that time to steady state grows.
findings.numbers: min = CPU count ms (capped), max = 50 ms; 2018: single thread, 10 ms

findings.claim: Since 2017 a single CodeVersionManager owns all code versions of a method: tiering, profiler ReJIT and diagnostics. IL belongs to a code version, not to the method. Before that, ReJIT, EnC, tiering and the IL interpreter each had their own dispatch-switching mechanism (JumpStamp, FixupPrecode, a custom stub).
findings.mechanism: Versions form a tree: ILCodeVersion -> NativeCodeVersion (per generic instantiation, with an optimization tier). The tiers are Tier0, Tier1, Tier1OSR, Optimized, Tier0Instrumented and Tier1Instrumented. A build pipeline lets stages (EnC, profiler, debugger, tiering) each add part of the config. A Tier1 version is bound to the IL version at queue time and is not activated if the IL changed in between (AsyncPromoteToTier1 comment). Unified lifetime management of code versions was a stated goal still unsolved in 2017.
findings.numbers: 6 optimization tiers in NativeCodeVersion::OptimizationTier

findings.topic: R2R as Tier0, rejit when hot
findings.claim: Precompiled R2R code counts as 'tier0'. When it gets hot (30 calls) it is rejitted. The rejit can use exact CPU features and the set of loaded dependencies, and since .NET 8 also profile data.
findings.mechanism: Tier0 is 'whatever code can be made available most quickly': R2R code if present, otherwise quick-JIT code. R2R code has no patchpoints and no instrumentation.
findings.numbers: threshold 30 calls (shared with jitted Tier0)

findings.claim: OSR places patchpoints at loop back-edge targets. A per-frame counter starts at 1000 and counts down. A patchpoint must call the helper 10 times before an OSR method is built. The OSR method is a partial method compiled for that one patchpoint, and it keeps the original Tier0 frame in place as part of its own frame.
findings.mechanism: Tier0 keeps all IL state in stack slots at IL-stack-empty points, so one patchpoint descriptor (all locals live) is enough and Tier0 needs no liveness pass. The helper returns a continuation address. The OSR frame keeps the original frame because address-exposed locals must stay at the same addresses. Transitions happen only for the frame on top of the stack. Patchpoint strategy defaults to 'adaptive' (2). Partial compilation is off (TC_PartialCompilation=0). OSR is jitted at the Tier1 level and reads the Tier0 profile.
findings.numbers: TC_OnStackReplacement_InitialCounter=1000, OSR_CounterBump=1000, OSR_HitLimit=10, TC_PatchpointStrategy=2

findings.claim: Before OSR, methods with loops skipped Tier0 and went straight to full optimization. That lost startup time, and later lost the Tier0 profile. .NET 7 turned on OSR, and with it TC_QuickJitForLoops, by default (dotnet/runtime#65675). At HEAD the default is 1 only when FEATURE_ON_STACK_REPLACEMENT is built in, and 0 otherwise.
findings.mechanism: Without OSR, a method called once with a long loop would be stuck in Tier0. On .NET 6, turning QuickJitForLoops on without OSR made a loop benchmark take 2.5x as long (Toub). OSR is rare but essential. In one large internal Microsoft web app, 55 of 195,188 jitted methods contained OSR.
findings.numbers: .NET 6 QuickJitForLoops w/o OSR: 2.5x slower on the loop example; 55 OSR methods / 195,188 jitted (0.03%)

findings.claim: CoreCLR has no general deoptimization out of optimized code. OSR goes only from unoptimized code to optimized code. The OSR design says 'we currently don't have any need to transfer control out of jitted optimized code (Tier1)'. It explains that deopt would need live-state preservation, rebuilding inlined frames, and limits on dead-store elimination and code motion.
findings.mechanism: Speculation is done with guards that have an in-line fallback path (GDV), never with deopt. A deopt into an interpreter would 'need to keep some of its state in the original method frame'.

findings.claim: GDV replaces a virtual or interface call with: if (type == likely) { direct, usually inlined, call } else { the original virtual call }. Before GDV, the JIT could devirtualize only about 15% of virtual call sites and about 5% of interface call sites.
findings.mechanism: Class profiles come from Tier0 class probes. The JIT may chain up to 5 type checks. The chain likelihood threshold is 75% (0x4B). By default a candidate is kept even if the target can't be inlined (RequireInlining=0, labelled as 'the legacy behavior' change). Casts, delegates and values (e.g. Buffer.Memmove size) are also profiled. JitRandomGuardedDevirtualization is a stress mode.
findings.numbers: pre-GDV devirt success 15% virtual / 5% interface; MAX_GDV_TYPE_CHECKS=5; chain likelihood 75

findings.claim: Each type probe is a fixed 32-entry reservoir sample with a sample interval of 64. It holds a count plus a table of type or method handles, with flags for class, interface or delegate.
findings.mechanism: HandleHistogram32 { Count; HandleTable[32] }. SAMPLE_INTERVAL / SIZE = average number of calls between table updates. A 64-bit variant exists. The JIT reads the table at Tier1 to pick GDV candidates. The DynamicPgo doc proposed 'randomized sampling to construct an approximate histogram'.
findings.numbers: SIZE=32, SAMPLE_INTERVAL=64

findings.claim: PR #70941 added instrumented tiers. Uninstrumented Tier0 becomes hot (30 calls), then goes to Tier0Instrumented, then to Tier1. Hot R2R code goes to Tier1Instrumented (optimized, with probes), then to Tier1. R2R code itself is never instrumented. Only hot code pays for probes.
findings.mechanism: AsyncPromoteToTier1 picks Tier1Instrumented for R2R because an unoptimized instrumented tier would 'produce a lot of new compilations for small methods which were inlined in R2R' and would be a 'noticeable performance regression from fast R2R to slow instrumented Tier0'. There is an exception for cold Tier0 methods with loops: CORJIT_FLAG_BBINSTR_IF_LOOPS instruments them, so the OSR version still has a profile. Known limit: instrumentation after R2R is weaker, because inlinees are not instrumented.
findings.numbers: AvaloniaILSpy start: 2.03 s (no PGO) -> 2.26 s (PGO, instrument all Tier0) -> 2.03 s (instrumented tiers); about 8% time-to-first-request cut across TechEmpower; about 10-20% of methods reach Tier1; 40-60% of methods < 8 B IL; instrumented tiers add about 13 MB in a 10 GB service (about 0.1%) and about 1 MB in AvaloniaILSpy

findings.claim: Dynamic PGO was opt-in in .NET 6 and 7 and is on by default since .NET 8. Microsoft reports about a 15% average gain. In a suite of about 4,600 benchmarks, 23% improved by 20% or more. Bing saw 13% fewer CPU cycles per query, but first had to deal with a rejit queue that grew past 300,000 methods.
findings.mechanism: Tier0 (or Tier1Instrumented) collects edge counts, class, cast, delegate and value histograms. Tier1 reads them for inlining, GDV, block layout and hot/cold splitting. Bing set DOTNET_TC_CallCountingDelayMs=0 and DOTNET_JitCollect64BitCounts=1, added warmup queries, and paused before taking traffic. Bing had tried NGEN and R2R 'to various levels of success' and settled on the JIT plus pre-jitting a list of critical methods.
findings.numbers: avg about 15%; 23% of about 4,600 tests >= 20%; Bing: -13% CPU, -20% queries hit by gen0/1 GC, about -8% overall serving time; rejit queue > 300,000

findings.claim: Plain shared 'racing' counters made Tier0-instrumented code 2-3x slower than uninstrumented Tier0 in heavily multithreaded apps, because of cache contention, and they also lost many updates. Interlocked counters fixed accuracy but cost more. The fix (2023) is probabilistic counting: once a count reaches 2^13, add 2^k with probability 2^-k.
findings.mechanism: ScalableProfileCount: for count >= 8192, delta = 1 << (log2(count) - 12), applied when (rand & (delta-1)) == 0. This follows Dice, Lev and Moir's 'Scalable Statistics Counters'. Counter placement uses a spanning tree (Ball-Larus), so only non-tree edges get probes. 64-bit counts are optional (JitCollect64BitCounts=0 by default).
findings.numbers: racing counters 2-3x slowdown; TieredPGO_ScalableCountThreshold=13 (log2); JitScalableProfiling=1

findings.claim: The PGO author warns that Tier0 may run 'as few as 30' times before Tier1, that phased behavior gives unrepresentative samples, and that an OSR method covering the whole rest of a method can leave later loops unprofiled. The doc suggests loop-body-only OSR 'used in JavaScript engines like Chakra'.
findings.mechanism: Profile data lives in a runtime slab. If the slab fills, later Tier0 methods are not instrumented. Tier1 can read counts while Tier0 is still writing them, so the counts may be inconsistent. Keying a profile across runs is 'surprisingly challenging': it uses token, hash and IL size.
findings.numbers: as few as 30 Tier0 executions

findings.claim: Static PGO reuses the dynamic path. You run with TieredPGO=1, TC_QuickJitForLoops=1, TC_CallCountThreshold=10000 and ReadyToRun=0, so methods stay instrumented longer. You trace the run, dotnet-pgo turns the trace into a .mibc file, and crossgen2 reads it (ReadyToRunOptimizationData). Mono's AOT compiler reads the same .mibc for profiled AOT on Android. The older IBC format worked only for first-party assemblies and lost most of its value when R2R replaced NGEN.
findings.mechanism: A .mibc file is a PE file whose IL encodes method groups and profile data. Mono resolves MethodRef and MethodSpec tokens from it to choose which methods to AOT. 'IBC count data is not currently available to the JIT', and 'the IBCMerge tool is not available externally'.
findings.numbers: collection run uses TC_CallCountThreshold=10000

findings.claim: A version bubble is 'a set of DLLs that we are willing to update as a set'. Inlining across bubbles is forbidden, except for methods marked [NonVersionable], whose owners give up the right to change the body. The runtime also freezes the layout of Object, arrays and String, because otherwise every field access would pay a versioning cost.
findings.mechanism: Field offsets of base types outside the bubble are loaded from fixup slots set up once (measured worst case < 1% in a 1K-node linked list). Cross-module calls are indirect. Interface dispatch across bubbles uses VSD. crossgen2 throws RequiresRuntimeJitException when an inlinee from outside the bubble touches fields outside the bubble, which leaves that method for the runtime JIT. With cross-bubble inlining off, plus [NonVersionable] on key methods, there was 'no visible regression in ASP.NET throughput'.
findings.numbers: cross-bubble field access overhead < 1% (contrived worst case)

findings.claim: R2R code carries assumptions as fixups that are checked lazily. Check_* fixups (type layout, field offset, instruction-set support, virtual override, IL body) silently drop that method's code, and the method is jitted instead. Verify_* fixups fail hard with a runtime exception.
findings.mechanism: The fixup is resolved before first use. Check_IL_Body lets cross-module-inlined code survive only if the inlinee's IL at runtime matches the IL seen at compile time. Check_InstructionSetSupport ties a method to CPU features. crossgen2's ShouldSkipCompilation skips methods whose instruction-set needs can't be expressed.
findings.numbers: fixup kinds 0x2A-0x36

findings.claim: R2R images record an inlinee -> inliners hashtable (CrossModuleInlineInfo, R2R 6.3+). When a profiler or EnC changes an inlinee, every R2R inliner can be found and invalidated. CoreCLR loads this section only in builds that support profiling, ReJIT or code versioning.
findings.mechanism: The hashtable is keyed by a version-resilient hash of the inlinee methoddef. The inliners are stored as delta-encoded RIDs (plus module ids in multi-module bubbles). The legacy InliningInfo section (v2.1) is 'no longer consumed'.

findings.topic: R2R compat: designed as a format, run as a cache
findings.claim: The R2R design (about 2014) promised a native format that keeps running across runtime updates, unlike NGEN, which was a cache thrown away on any change. In practice, at HEAD both the minimum and the current major version are 34, so an image with any other major version is rejected ('Ready to Run disabled - unsupported header version') and the IL is jitted instead. The 2020 composite design states the principle directly: 'R2R file is a code cache.'
findings.mechanism: The header version history lists many breaking majors (3.0, 6.0, 16, 17, 29 are marked 'not backward compatible'), driven by ABI, GC info and debug-info changes. This is safe only because the IL ships next to the code. R2R 18.5 added READYTORUN_FLAG_STRIPPED_IL_BODIES, which removes that safety net.
findings.numbers: READYTORUN_MAJOR_VERSION 34 = MINIMUM_READYTORUN_MAJOR_VERSION 34

findings.claim: Composite R2R compiles many assemblies into one native image, which forms one large version bubble. That gives tighter codegen, large pages and simpler deployment. The original IL and metadata are kept next to it or embedded in it, so reflection and fallback still work. In .NET 11, iOS and Mac Catalyst use composite R2R: partial in Debug, full in Release.
findings.mechanism: Component assemblies point to their OwnerCompositeExecutable. 'Full ReadyToRun doesn't guarantee that every method is precompiled; the CoreCLR interpreter executes methods that aren't precompiled.'

findings.claim: ILC is a dependency-graph compiler. It starts from roots and adds static, conditional ('B if A and C') and dynamic dependencies. Only reached nodes get code. A virtual method body is emitted only if its slot is used and its type is actually constructed. Generic virtual methods need the costly dynamic dependencies.
findings.mechanism: Constructed and unconstructed type nodes are modelled separately and merged when the object file is written. GVMDependenciesNode watches which types get constructed and adds the overrides that apply. Shadow method nodes carry per-instantiation dependencies for shared canonical code (__Canon). --dgmllog dumps the graph.

findings.claim: ILC can run an IL scanner first: a 'compilation with a null code generation backend' that builds a strict superset of the real graph. Its results (lazy vtable slot assignment, devirtualization facts) feed the real compile. The compiler itself is 'policy free': the driver picks the policies for vtables, devirtualization, reflection metadata and stack-trace data, so the same core can serve full AOT and mixed JIT modes.
findings.mechanism: Scanning breaks the chicken-and-egg problem of whole-program optimization: you need the program's shape before optimizing any part. It is optional when compile time matters more. VTableSliceProvider can be chosen per type, for example to allow lazy vtables even with a JIT present for types the JIT can't see.

findings.claim: NativeAOT's whole-program view allows optimizations that are illegal with a JIT. A class with no loaded subclasses is treated as sealed and its virtual calls are inlined. An interface with two implementors gets a type test plus inlining. A static constructor is interpreted at compile time and its readonly results are folded to constants. The author says the JIT usually wins peak throughput, but 'these closed world optimizations can sometimes give edge to the AOT-compiled one'.
findings.mechanism: With a JIT, 'at any point Derived could be loaded', which would need a fallback or code invalidation. JIT .NET instead has dynamic PGO.

findings.claim: NativeAOT gives up dynamic loading, Reflection.Emit, C++/CLI and built-in COM. It requires trimming and single-file output. LINQ expression trees always run interpreted. Every struct generic instantiation is pre-generated, and GVMs get an instantiation per overriding type, which 'can have significant impact to the disk size'. Library authors must annotate code (IsAotCompatible, trim and AOT analyzers), and reflection-heavy frameworks need source generators instead (System.Text.Json, P/Invoke). MVC and Blazor Server are still not supported.
findings.mechanism: The analyzers warn at build and publish time. Features that are not compatible 'are disabled and throw exceptions at run time'. RuntimeFeature.IsDynamicCodeSupported=false lets you test the fallback paths under the JIT.

findings.claim: .NET 8 ASP.NET Core numbers. Simple API: startup 156 -> 48 ms, size 92.6 -> 10.0 MB, working set 96 -> 41 MB. Complex API: 473 -> 115 ms, 98.27 -> 21.55 MB, 193 -> 121 MB. A Hello World on Linux x64 (stripped) is 1.84 MB on .NET 8, down from 3.76 MB on .NET 7. On iOS versus Mono: about 35% smaller and about 28% faster startup; .NET MAUI iOS up to 50% for both.
findings.mechanism: No JIT, no IL, pre-built type structures, trimming. The cost is no dynamic PGO, so the runtime can't recompile from observed behavior.
findings.numbers: see claim; no official AOT-vs-JIT RPS figure found (a 3rd-party blog reports 396k vs 412k req/s, est., not verified)

findings.claim: In Mono, iOS release builds are full AOT by default. Without the interpreter, any attempt to JIT throws ExecutionEngineException ('Attempting to JIT compile method while running in aot-only mode'). UseInterpreter / MtouchInterpreter lets you mix AOT and interpreted code per assembly (e.g. '-all,System.Numerics'). Costs: slower code, and native crash stacks show generic interpreter frames.
findings.mechanism: Full AOT must also emit 'extra' methods (generic instances, wrappers) and all trampolines. For trampolines needed in unbounded numbers, one code page is mapped many times next to writable data pages. Mono AOT images need exact GUID matches of the input assemblies and every reference, otherwise they don't load.

findings.claim: In .NET 11 and later, CoreCLR is the runtime for .NET MAUI on iOS and Mac Catalyst. Composite R2R covers precompiled code, and the CoreCLR interpreter is 'always enabled and executes code that isn't precompiled'. NativeAOT stays a separate model with no interpreter. The Mono knobs (UseInterpreter, MtouchInterpreter) don't apply.
findings.mechanism: The R2R format gained support for this: R2R 18.7 READYTORUN_HELPER_R2RToInterpreter, plus Wasm signature-string thunks shared by crossgen2, WasmAppBuilder and the runtime. RyuJIT gained a wasm backend (codegenwasm.cpp, emitwasm.cpp, lowerwasm.cpp, regallocwasm.cpp …) for R2R on WebAssembly.

findings.topic: Mono wasm AOT: always-available interpreter, EH via 'deopt'
findings.claim: On wasm, Mono supports only two modes: interpreter, or AOT plus interpreter, so falling back to the interpreter is always possible. AOT code (Mono LLVM backend -> emscripten) can't walk the stack. So it keeps an IL-level shadow state (IL offset plus all IL variables) updated as it runs. When it catches an exception, it hands that state to the interpreter, which runs the EH code. The runtime code calls this 'deopt'.
findings.mechanism: Calls from AOT code that might land in the interpreter are indirect, with aot->interp and interp->aot wrappers per signature. GC refs in AOT frames are stored in a gc_pin area in the linear-memory C stack, so the GC scans and pins them. Null checks are explicit because wasm has no signals.

findings.claim: The jiterpreter compiles hot traces of Mono interpreter opcodes into small wasm modules. A trace goes prepare point -> hit threshold -> synchronous compile -> monitor point. While monitored it builds a penalty score from early exits, and is then either kept (patched to ENTER) or turned into a NOP. It is limited by the browsers' 4 KB limit on synchronously compiled modules, a total wasm-bytes budget, and an automatic shutoff after repeated compile errors.
findings.mechanism: Two passes: opcode translation (native wasm, C helper, libc call, or bailout), then a control-flow pass that builds structured wasm, with a dispatch table for back edges. Each opcode has a 'value' score, and a trace whose total is below the threshold is rejected. Null-check facts are thrown away at every branch. Notes on cost: one wasm branch per interpreter branch predicts worse (interpreter error branches predict about 99% right), traces can evict the interpreter's hot cache lines, and browsers' baseline wasm tiers must also handle the output well.
findings.numbers: 4 KB sync module limit; jiterpreter-wasm-bytes-limit cap; traces on by default only in single-threaded builds

findings.claim: Green nodes are immutable and store no position or parent: only kind, width, children and diagnostics. They are shared within a tree and across trees, so the green structure is really a DAG. Red nodes are lazy wrappers that compute position and parent. An incremental reparse reuses green nodes as the same objects in memory.
findings.mechanism: Tokens, trivia and lists are green objects but red structs, so they cost no red allocations. Lists of 0, 1 and 2-4 elements have special forms (null, direct child, WithTwo/Three/FourChildren). A green node cache (65,536 entries, nodes with <= 3 children) and pre-cached keywords and trivia remove duplicates. Large method body blocks hold their red children weakly.
findings.numbers: tokens, lists and trivia >= 75% of elements; >= 90% of lists have <= 4 elements; cache 65,536 entries, 55% hit rate; incremental reuse 'approaching 99.99%'

findings.claim: Roslyn has three semantic layers. The internal bound tree follows the program's static semantics and must 'capture all semantic information' (no going back to syntax). Lowering passes rewrite it. IOperation plus ControlFlowGraph is a separate public, language-neutral (C#/VB) semantic API for analyzers. A test hook checks every syntax node against it.
findings.mechanism: Lowering order in LowerBodyOrInitializer: LocalRewriter -> extension rewriters -> AsyncExceptionHandlerRewriter -> ClosureConversion -> IteratorRewriter -> AsyncRewriter or RuntimeAsyncRewriter -> emit. PipelinePhaseValidator asserts, in DEBUG builds only, which node kinds may still exist after each phase (InitialBinding, LocalRewriting, Spilling, ClosureConversion, StateMachineRewriting, Emit). Under ROSLYN_TEST_IOPERATION, every syntax node gets GetOperation plus a CFG verify. A new BoundKind must get IOperation support in the same PR.
findings.numbers: OperationInterfaces.xml: 142 node definitions; ControlFlowGraphBuilder.cs 8,142 lines

findings.claim: ISourceGenerator (v1) is deprecated. IIncrementalGenerator replaced it: a pipeline of small transforms whose outputs are cached and compared by value between runs. That requires deterministic steps, and the docs advise extracting value-type data early and not caching symbols. Generators are also how .NET replaced runtime reflection for AOT (JSON, P/Invoke, Regex).
findings.mechanism: 'incremental generators actively _require_' determinism. Each Select/Where step is a checkpoint. If the cached input compares equal, the rest of the work is skipped.

findings.topic: Runtime async: a lowering moves from front end to JIT
findings.claim: Async state machine lowering is moving out of Roslyn and into the runtime. With runtime async on, Roslyn runs RuntimeAsyncRewriter instead of AsyncRewriter. The JIT compiles with CORJIT_FLAG_ASYNC and handles suspension and continuations. An ECMA-335 augment draft defines the IL contract.
findings.mechanism: IsRuntimeAsyncEnabledIn(method) picks the rewriter. The code generator must recognize call + optional ConfigureAwait + AsyncHelpers.Await sequences and save and restore ExecutionContext and SynchronizationContext. R2R 20, 25 and 29 bumped the format for async debug info and Wasm async resume.

findings.claim: Every tiering mechanism has a stress or force knob, and debug builds use tiny thresholds. Examples: debug call threshold 2 with a 1 ms delay; TC_AggressiveTiering; JitRandomOnStackReplacement and JitOffsetOnStackReplacement; OSR range filters; JitRandomGuardedDevirtualization; JitRandomEdgeCounts; JitRandomPartialCompilation; TC_DeleteCallCountingStubsAfter. The OSR prototype passed pri0 tests with 'produce the OSR method and transition the first time each patchpoint is hit'.
findings.mechanism: 'Design for testability. We should be able to force OSR transitions wherever possible and with alternative stress strategies' is one of the OSR design principles.

lessons.lesson: .NET makes every executor go through one narrow, versioned interface over one IR: IL to ICorJitInfo, about 184 calls, one GUID. Even the interpreter is a 'JIT' that can answer SKIPPED. ep9 already keeps the AST inside ep9_frontend and treats CompiledUnit as the cache and unit format (H01). The step still open: give T0, T1, T2 and the AOT compiler one shared runtime-query trait (shapes, feedback, fuses, builtins), versioned by one id that every compiler checks at load. 'May decline this function' should be a normal result, not an error. Then a new tier, or the jitless lowering, is a plug-in and not a fork.

Express modes as flags plus a policy object passed to one compiler. Don't fork the compiler per mode. RyuJIT serves JIT, R2R and NativeAOT with CORJIT flags plus 62 ABI and R2R checks. ILC's core is 'policy free', and its driver picks vtable, devirtualization and metadata policy. For ep9: the jit, jitless, hybrid and AOT presets (plan 13 L-B ExecOptions) should feed one lowering pipeline with a mode word. Keep a grep-able count of mode branches in the compilers, because that count is the team's maintenance bill.

Treat an AOT unit as a cache that always keeps its bytecode, and guard its assumptions per function. R2R's promise of a lasting format fell back to 'code cache': major 34 == minimum 34, and older images are simply rejected. That stays safe only because IL ships alongside. Check_* fixups drop one method to the JIT, and Verify_* fail hard. ep9's H35 field-by-field fallback (native mismatch -> unit bytecode) matches this. Keep two separate outcomes, 'drop to bytecode quietly' and 'clean load error', and never ship a unit without bytecode in a mode that can re-tier or deopt (R2R's STRIPPED_IL_BODIES gives up exactly that safety).

Cross-unit inlining needs a boundary rule and a reverse map. In R2R, inlining stops at the version bubble unless a method is marked NonVersionable. A Check_IL_Body fixup checks each inlined body at load. An inlinee -> inliners table lets a changed callee find every inliner. ep9's reserved `deps` section (inlined units plus digests, F11) covers the check. Also add the reverse index (inlinee -> inliner functions), so a hot-patched or re-evaluated callee can invalidate AOT inliners without scanning every unit. And define what a 'bubble' is (one ep9c invocation, one app snapshot?) before A3 turns on cross-unit inlining.

Re-tier hot AOT code through an optimized instrumented tier, and instrument only hot code. .NET learned that sending hot R2R code back to unoptimized instrumented Tier0 causes a flood of new compiles and a speed drop. It also learned that instrumenting every Tier0 method cost startup (2.03 -> 2.26 s), and fixed it by instrumenting only after the method is hot. ep9's H33 path (optimized-AOT -> instrumented T1 -> T2) matches. Also copy two details: (a) T0 should create a feedback vector only once a function is hot, which ep9 already does with threshold 8; (b) the BBINSTR_IF_LOOPS exception, so a cold function with a hot loop still gets a profile before OSR into T2.

Add a 'startup phase' rule to tiering. .NET waits 100 ms of no new Tier0 activity before counting calls, and the delay re-arms on every new burst. It paces background compiles with an adaptive slice of 1-50 ms. Without the delay, counting and background compiles slowed startup enough to wipe out the Tier0 win. Bing shows the opposite risk: delay set to 0 plus a huge app meant a rejit queue over 300,000 methods. Grepping ep9's plan and ADRs found no startup-delay or compile-queue policy. For the A4 tuning gate, measure SHORT-RUN (tsc 1-2 s) with and without a re-arming delay, and add a queue-length cap or drop policy.

OSR came before 'baseline for every function'. Until .NET 7, methods with loops skipped Tier0, because without OSR a long loop got stuck in slow code (2.5x slower). OSR is used rarely (0.03% of methods) but it is what made the default safe. ep9 already makes every JumpLoop budget poll a lazy-deopt point with full metadata (H29). Check that T0 -> T2 loop OSR entry exists and is stress-tested before tier-up thresholds are tuned. Also note .NET's open problem: an OSR method that covers the rest of the function means later loops never get profiled. Chakra-style loop-body OSR is the fix their doc suggests.

CoreCLR shows how far you can get with guards that have an in-line fallback and no deopt: GDV with up to 5 type checks, a 75% likelihood bar, and the original virtual call in the else branch. JS needs deopt in JIT mode, but in jitless and AOT-optimized modes ep9 has no T1 to deopt into and is limited to SLOWPATH (H32). Use the GDV shape there: guard -> inlined fast path, else the generic IC call, plus an exit counter. Keep deopt for the JIT tiers. GDV's 32-entry reservoir histogram (sampled every 64 calls) is a cheap model for polymorphic call feedback when feedback is written by baseline-AOT IC cells.

Closed-world AOT wins (seal a class with no subclasses, devirtualize interfaces with few implementors, run static constructors at build time) are legal only with no dynamic code. NativeAOT pays for that with no Reflection.Emit, no Assembly.Load, required trimming, and per-instantiation code growth. ep9 must keep eval and new Function in every mode (H05), so its world is never closed. Turn each whole-program fact into a fuse-guarded assumption (H31 InvalidatingFuse), not a proof. Borrow ILC's tools anyway: a scan pass with no codegen that builds a reachability graph with conditional edges (a method only if its shape is constructed). It feeds the AOT inliner and the snapshot, and its dump (--dgmllog) explains size.

Watch code size from specialization. NativeAOT warns that every struct generic instantiation and every GVM override gets its own code, with 'significant impact to the disk size'. Instrumented tiers roughly double Tier1 code size (10-20% of methods reach Tier1). For ep9, specializing AOT code per shape or element kind, and keeping baseline-AOT and optimized-AOT variants of the same function, multiplies the same way. Put a per-unit size budget and a variant count in the A2/A3 gates, as .NET tracks Tier0/Tier1/OSR MB per app.

Use one profile schema for dynamic and static PGO, keyed by stable identity. .NET reuses the same instrumentation to make .mibc files (dotnet-pgo), feeds them to crossgen2 and to Mono AOT, and found that keying across runs (token + hash + IL size) is 'surprisingly challenging'. Its legacy IBC failed because it was a separate, first-party-only path. ep9's stable function ids plus content hash (H01) and the shared feedback schema (H33) are the right base. Let a run export the FeedbackVector state as a PROFILED side file in the same schema as .ep9h hints (H37), with the runtime > PROFILED > HINTED order already decided. Racing-counter loss is minor in a single-threaded isolate, but 64-bit or saturating counters matter for hot loops.

On iOS and wasm, an interpreter must always be there behind AOT code, and the boundary is the hard part. .NET 11 moved iOS from Mono to CoreCLR composite R2R plus an always-on interpreter. Mono wasm AOT keeps an IL-level shadow state so it can 'deopt' into the interpreter for exception handling, because wasm can't walk the stack. The jiterpreter shows the limits of JIT inside wasm: 4 KB sync modules, a byte budget, a penalty-based keep/NOP decision, and auto-shutoff. For ep9: per-signature AOT<->interpreter thunks generated at build time, a unit-to-interpreter helper, and frame state that the interpreter can resume from. Design these before the wasm target, not after.

A front end gains from immutable, shareable nodes and checks between phases. Roslyn's green nodes have no position or parent, so they are shared and reused across edits (55% cache hits). The public semantic API (IOperation) is kept apart from the internal bound tree. A DEBUG-only PipelinePhaseValidator asserts which node kinds may still exist after each lowering pass. ep9 keeps the oxc AST private (H01). Add a debug validator between ep9_frontend's lowering steps and BytecodeGen ('no X after pass Y'). Also add an always-on test hook that walks every function's ScopeAnalysis and bytecode and checks invariants over the whole test262 corpus, as ROSLYN_TEST_IOPERATION does.

Build force and stress knobs into every transition from day one. .NET's debug builds use threshold 2 and a 1 ms delay. It has random OSR placement, random GDV, random edge counts and per-method range filters, and the OSR prototype was proven with 'transition at first hit'. ep9 should have matching knobs (tier-up at call 1, OSR at every JumpLoop, deopt at every guard, fuse pop on every check, function-id range filters) and run test262 under each in CI. That is the cheap way to cover the T0/T1/T2/AOT x deopt/OSR matrix.

Unify code versioning and dispatch early, and keep the IR high enough that back ends can choose the lowering. CoreCLR spent about 20 years with separate ReJIT, EnC, tiering and interpreter switching before CodeVersionManager (2017). It ran two runtimes (CoreCLR and Mono) until .NET 11, and its new interpreter still can't tier. It is now moving async lowering from Roslyn into the JIT (runtime async). For ep9: one code-object and version record per function (bytecode version -> code kind/tier -> dispatch slot), shared by T1/T2 install, AOT load, lazy deopt slot swap and debugger. And bytecode that keeps generator/async suspend points as ops, so a future T2 or AOT can lower them its own way.

failures_and_reversals: Tiered compilation: prototyped 2016, opt-in in .NET Core 2.1 and 2.2 (off by default), on by default in .NET Core 3.0 (learn.microsoft.com runtime-config/compilation; tiered-compilation.md:42).

QuickJitForLoops: off by default from 3.0 to 6. Methods with loops went straight to full optimization, which cost startup and later the Tier0 profile. On .NET 6, turning it on without OSR made a loop benchmark 2.5x slower. .NET 7 turned on OSR and QuickJitForLoops by default (dotnet/runtime#65675, Toub .NET 7 perf post). Docs vs code: Learn's compilation page still says an omitted QuickJitForLoops means false, but clrconfigvalues.h:480 defaults it to 1 when OSR is built in.

The 2.1 tiering delay was a one-shot 100 ms timer that never restarted, a known issue for servers that go idle and then jit heavily again. It became a 'perpetual' delay that re-arms on new Tier0 activity (clrconfigvalues.h:486; tieredcompilation.cpp:120-160).

Call counting in the prestub ('utterly naive', high per-call cost, 2018 doc) was replaced by call counting stubs that are deleted in bulk afterwards (callcounting.h). The fixed 10 ms background compile chunk was replaced by an adaptive 1-50 ms slice.

Dynamic PGO: opt-in in .NET 6 and 7, default in .NET 8. First version: R2R code was never profiled, so framework-heavy apps saw no gain, and instrumenting all Tier0 regressed startup (AvaloniaILSpy 2.03 -> 2.26 s). Fix: instrumented tiers, instrumenting only hot code, with hot R2R going to Tier1Instrumented (PR #70941).

Racing (unsynchronized) PGO counters made instrumented code 2-3x slower under contention and lost updates. Interlocked counters were more accurate but slower. Both were replaced in 2023 by scalable approximate counting above 2^13.

Bing on .NET 8: the PGO rejit queue grew past 300,000 methods before the first user query and caused a first-query latency spike. Fixes were warmup, a pause before traffic, DOTNET_TC_CallCountingDelayMs=0 and 64-bit counters. Earlier NGEN and R2R attempts gave 'various levels of success'.
IBC (legacy PGO for NGEN and crossgen): first-party only, counts never reached the JIT, and most of the benefit was lost with R2R. It was superseded by dotnet-pgo and .mibc.

NGEN was a fragile cache. R2R (about 2014) was designed as a format with 'a strong guarantee' of running across updates. In practice the major version has been bumped incompatibly many times, and at HEAD MINIMUM == MAJOR == 34, so the composite design (2020) restated 'R2R file is a code cache'. The legacy InliningInfo section is no longer read.
ILC dropped its CppCodegen backend (IL -> C++ for quick platform bring-up). It was not brought over from the archived CoreRT repo, and LLVM/wasm lives in a runtimelab branch.

Two runtimes: Mono (full AOT plus interpreter for iOS, wasm and Android) alongside CoreCLR for years. NativeAOT on iOS appeared experimentally in .NET 8. In .NET 11, CoreCLR (composite R2R plus an always-on interpreter) replaces Mono on iOS and Mac Catalyst, and the Mono UseInterpreter and MtouchInterpreter knobs no longer apply. RyuJIT gained a wasm backend.

The old CoreCLR IL interpreter (off by default, 2018) was replaced by a new CoreCLR interpreter built as an ICorJitCompiler. At HEAD (2026-11), turning on the interpreter turns tiered compilation off ('do not work well together currently').

Before CodeVersionManager (2017), ReJIT (JumpStamp), EnC and tiering (FixupPrecode) and the interpreter (custom stub) each switched code their own way. They were unified after about 20 years. Unified lifetime management of code versions was still listed as unsolved.

Roslyn: ISourceGenerator (v1) is deprecated in favor of incremental generators, because v1 re-ran too often at IDE scale. Async state machines are moving from Roslyn lowering (AsyncRewriter) to runtime async in the JIT (RuntimeAsyncRewriter + CORJIT_FLAG_ASYNC; the ECMA-335 augment is still a draft).

OSR open issues the team names: OSR methods cover the whole rest of the method, so multi-loop methods may never profile later loops. Partial compilation is still off by default (TC_PartialCompilation=0). Deopt out of Tier1 is not built, by choice.

system: Kotlin (K2/FIR front end, one shared IR with ordered lowerings, klib, Kotlin/Native LLVM AOT and its runtime/GC, Kotlin/JS IR, Kotlin/Wasm GC), plus Kotlin/JVM on HotSpot tiered C1/C2 and OpenJDK Leyden (JEP 483/514/515/544, and jaotc JEP 295/410). Sources: a sparse clone of JetBrains/kotlin (commit c2edd73dd8e7, 2026-11-18; cited as kotlin@c2edd73d:path:line); openjdk.org JEP pages fetched 2026-11-18; HotSpot compiler_globals.hpp and compilationPolicy.hpp from openjdk/jdk master on 2026-11-18; kotlinlang.org docs and JetBrains blog posts fetched 2026-11-18 (current Kotlin 2.4.21). I also read the ep9 tree (m9-p5) only to map lessons: docs/adr/H33, H35, docs/plan/13. No ep9 doc mentions Kotlin, so this is new ground. Leyden is already in docs/research/11-dual-mode-vms.md; I only add the parts that are new there.

findings.claim: FIR is the front-end tree. Resolution runs as a fixed, ordered list of phases (RAW_FIR, IMPORTS, SUPER_TYPES, TYPES, STATUS, CONTRACTS, IMPLICIT_TYPES_BODY_RESOLVE, BODY_RESOLVE, CHECKERS, then FIR2IR). The contract: an element seen in phase B is already resolved to every earlier phase A. The CLI runs the phases in order over the whole module. The IDE (Analysis API) runs them lazily, per declaration.
findings.mechanism: Errors found during resolution are stored in the tree. They are reported as diagnostics only in the CHECKERS phase. Code must read declarations through symbols (symbol.resolvedReturnTypeRef), not through the raw FIR element, so that a lazy mode can resolve the declaration on demand. One phase contract therefore serves both batch and lazy use.
sources: kotlin@c2edd73d:docs/fir/fir-basics.md:70-107 (symbol access rule for lazy Analysis API)

findings.claim: Kotlin 2.0 (May 2024) shipped K2 as stable. JetBrains claims it compiles 'twice as fast', and says 'all compiler backends now share a lot of logic and a unified pipeline', so features and fixes are done once for all platforms. The old frontend still lingers in 2026: the Native second stage still runs a K1 frontend phase to build the Objective-C framework header.
findings.mechanism: runK1Frontend throws if the language version uses K2 and source roots are present. ObjC export still needs K1 descriptors for klib metadata (produceObjCFramework calls runK1Frontend). The swift-export doc lists 'tied to descriptors that are a K1 legacy' as a cost. In Kotlin 2.3, KT-76344 dropped language version 1.9 for non-JVM targets.
findings.numbers: 'twice as fast' / 'potentially doubling it' is the vendor's claim, with 'some projects ... a bit slower'. IDE K2 mode: about 1.8x faster highlighting and 1.5x faster completion on the IntelliJ Ultimate codebase (vendor).
sources: https://blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2024/05/celebrating-kotlin-2-0-fast-smart-and-multiplatform/ (sections 'Faster compilation speed', 'Multiplatform from the ground up')

findings.claim: FIR becomes one backend IR (IrElement trees) through FIR2IR. On the JVM, the same compiler run applies the common and JVM lowerings and writes .class files. On Native, JS and Wasm, the first stage runs only 'pre-serialization lowerings' and writes a klib (serialized IR plus metadata). A second stage deserializes and links the klibs, runs the common and backend lowerings, and generates code.
findings.mechanism: The split is a switch in the pipeline ('Is this JVM compilation'). Klib is the shared portable artifact for three backends. Only the JVM skips it, because the .class file is its portable unit.

findings.claim: Each backend is an ordered list of named IR-to-IR passes. In this checkout the Native list references 80 lowerings, JVM 98, JS 119 and Wasm 92. backend.common holds 48 shared lowering files. On Native, the inliner (inlineAllFunctionsPhase) is a 'physical barrier' between two lists, and some passes are turned on per mode with takeIf { optimizationsEnabled } or takeIf { isCache }.
findings.mechanism: Each phase is a NamedCompilerPhase with pre- and post-actions: an IR dumper and an IR validator with type checks (getDefaultIrActions). backend.common has stage-specific validators: after private inlining only non-private call sites may remain; after first-stage inlining, unbound symbols are allowed; in the second stage, no inline call sites may remain. Some checks are still commented out (KT-68663, KT-80065).
findings.numbers: Counts are grep counts of '::Name' references in each phase file. They are approximate (est. ±5) because some are conditional.

findings.topic: JVM backend leaves speculation to HotSpot
findings.claim: The JVM lowering list does desugaring and layout work (inline classes, bytecode-inliner support, default args). It has no devirtualization, escape analysis or whole-program DCE pass. Those exist only in the Native backend, and Wasm and JS have their own DCE. On the JVM, Kotlin relies on HotSpot C2 for speculative optimization.
findings.mechanism: grep for devirt/escape in JvmLoweringPhases.kt finds nothing. The Native optimizations/ directory holds DevirtualizationAnalysis, EscapeAnalysis and DCE, and backend.wasm has a dce/ directory. The JVM IR backend became the default in Kotlin 1.5 (KT-44021).

findings.claim: A klib holds serialized Kotlin metadata plus serialized backend IR (the resolved AST). It is the publishable unit for Native, JS and Wasm. klib binaries reached Stable in Kotlin 1.9.20 (Nov 2023). The guarantee is one-way: backward compatible from 1.9.20 on (a 2.0.x compiler reads 1.9.2x klibs), with no forward guarantee. cinterop klibs are still Beta, with no cross-version guarantee.
findings.mechanism: Linking uses IdSignatures: a mangled declaration name plus a hash, with a signature version. The klib tool can dump-abi (one line per declaration) and dump signatures at a chosen -signature-version, so ABI changes show up as diffable text.

findings.topic: Partial linkage instead of link failure
findings.claim: Since Kotlin 1.9.0, when a klib references a declaration that is missing or changed, Native no longer fails the build. The linker patches the IR so that the broken expression or declaration throws a linkage error at run time, 'exactly as on the JVM'. Since 1.9.20 these issues are reported silently by default. -Xpartial-linkage-loglevel=WARNING or ERROR raises the level.
findings.mechanism: PartiallyLinkedIrTreePatcher replaces affected bodies and expressions with throwLinkageError(...). PartialLinkageCase lists about 20 causes (MissingDeclaration, UnusableClassifier, ExcessiveArguments, InvalidSamConversion, AbstractClassInstantiation, ...). The Native compiler cache stores the partial-linkage issues per library (savePartialLinkageIssues) so they replay without re-reading the IR.

findings.claim: Inline functions behave differently by backend. On the JVM, the callee body is copied into the caller's bytecode at library compile time, so a later dependency version does not change it ('lib.v1'). On klib backends the call was stored as a normal call and inlined after linking ('lib.v2'). The team chose the JVM model and is moving klib inlining before serialization (KT-64570). Old klibs stay on the late model as accepted tech debt.
findings.mechanism: Reasons from the design doc: the JVM model 'exists longer', the klib model is 'not reasonably implementable on JVM', and the JVM model is more intuitive and simpler. The new pipeline is: pre-inline lowerings, then IR inliner, then klib serializer, which must accept 'partially unbound IR'. Pre-inline lowerings now run before serialization, so they become part of the klib ABI.

findings.claim: A K/N binary always holds a transitively closed set of klibs, stdlib included. 'Two different binaries can't share any code', for example as a shared native library. Release ('link') is a global compile of the whole world.
findings.mechanism: The second stage takes all klibs and emits one LLVM module ('It won't be linked with any other LLVM module, so we can hide and DCE unused symbols'). The K/N runtime (GC and so on) is compiled to bitcode, linked into that module and optimized with it. Runtime functions such as safepoints can therefore be inlined into user code.

findings.topic: Global optimizations need the closed world
findings.claim: Native runs its whole-program passes (DFG build, devirtualization, DCE, global hierarchy analysis, escape analysis) only when optimizing and when no library comes from a static cache: runGlobalOptimizations = optimize && !cachedLibraries.hasStaticCaches. In the other direction, an optimized build ignores compiler caches 'with global optimizations' unless enableReleaseBinaryCache is set (default false).
findings.mechanism: runCodegen gates each pass with disable = !runGlobalOptimizations. GHAPhase is also disabled when producing a cache. ignoreCacheReason is set when optimizationsEnabled && !enableReleaseBinaryCache. So caches give fast debug builds, release builds are slow and uncached, and no mode has both.

findings.claim: K/N devirtualization uses Variable Type Analysis (Sundaresan et al., OOPSLA 2000) over a whole-program data-flow graph. A virtual or interface call site is rewritten only if it has at most 3 possible callees (IR_DEVIRTUALIZED_VTABLE_CALL = IR_DEVIRTUALIZED_ITABLE_CALL = 3). Graph building uses an unfold factor of 5. With 1 callee it becomes a direct call. With 2 or 3 it becomes a type-info compare chain, and in optimize mode the last case is NOT checked. With 0 callees the call becomes a throw.
findings.mechanism: Because the world is closed, the analysis proves the receiver set, so there is no miss path and no deopt. The proof is the guard. Checks are ordered by a small backtracking search: exact-type compare (weight 0), class subtype check (1), interface check (2). The constraint solver's greedy phase is capped at maxNumberOfIterations = 2. With no entry point (a library), every public function and every vtable/itable entry is a root, which weakens the result.
findings.numbers: unfold factor 3 (IR) and 5 (DFG); 2 greedy iterations

findings.topic: Global hierarchy analysis: closed-world layout plus an in-band fallback
findings.claim: K/N colors the interface conflict graph: two interfaces are connected if some class implements both. Each interface id holds its color in the low bits, so every class gets a perfect-hash itable. An interface call is then itable[id & (size-1)].vtable[m] and an interface check is itable[id & (size-1)].id == id. Class subtype checks use DFS enter/exit intervals. Tables are capped at 2^5 = 32 entries (MAX_BITS_PER_COLOR = 5).
findings.mechanism: There is a fallback in the same binary format: a negative interfaceTableSize means 'sorted table, binary search' (LookupInterfaceTableRecord). The fast path is emitted unconditionally only when GHA ran, the colors fit, and the output is not a FRAMEWORK. Otherwise the code tests the sign bit. GHA is disabled for caches. A closed-world layout trick thus has an open-world slow path that the same code can select.
findings.numbers: MAX_BITS_PER_COLOR = 5 (32-entry table)

findings.claim: K/N escape analysis computes five lifetimes (Stack, Local, Return value, Parameter, Global), but 'only Stack and Global lifetimes are supported by the codegen', so the other three become Global. Stack arrays share a budget of 65,536 bytes per function, smallest first ('TODO: To a setting?'). Objects of classes with finalizers never go on the stack. The analysis is interprocedural: a call-graph condensation in reverse topological order, using devirtualization results.
findings.mechanism: If a strongly connected component does not converge, a pessimistic result is used (DivergenceResolutionParams: MaxAttempts = 3, NegligibleSize = 100, SwellingFactor = 25). The shadow-stack root scanner still carries 'TODO: This is currently incompatible with stack-allocated objects', a sign of how GC rooting and EA interact.
findings.numbers: 65,536 B stack budget; MaxAttempts 3; 5 lifetimes defined, 2 used

findings.topic: What 'no JIT' costs on Native: generics and boxing
findings.claim: K/N does not specialize generics. Generic code works on boxed values. Lowerings include Autoboxing and GenericCallsReturnTypeEraser. ComputeTypesPass runs because the 'Inliner erases generics. Trying to restore some of the information'. Small boxed values come from preallocated BoxCache ranges. Without a JIT there is no runtime type feedback to undo this, so only static passes (inlining, ComputeTypes run twice, CastsOptimization) can win it back.
findings.mechanism: Value (inline) classes are a static-type tool: UnboxInlineLowering and InlineClassPropertyAccessorsLowering on Native, JvmInlineClassLowering on the JVM. They only work because the static type is sound.

findings.topic: Static-initializer checks: whole-program DFA (Native) vs two code versions (Leyden)
findings.claim: K/N initializes globals lazily, once per file (the new-MM default). It removes or hoists the per-call 'is this file initialized' checks with a three-step interprocedural data-flow analysis. JEP 544 has the same problem in AOT code but no closed world, so C2 compiles two versions of a method: a slow one with class-init checks and a fast one without. HotSpot switches to the fast one once all referenced classes are initialized.
findings.mechanism: Native: StaticInitializersOptimization computes the 'definitely initialized files' sets after a function returns, before its body, and at each call site. Leyden: two versions plus a runtime switch. AOT code also cannot constant-fold static finals, because no class is initialized at AOT time.
sources: https://openjdk.org/jeps/544 (Description: slow/fast versions; static final fields)

findings.claim: For debug binaries, each dependency klib is compiled once to a static library (.a) under ~/.konan. Side files stored with it let the compiler skip reading that klib's IR: class field layouts, inline function bodies, eager-initialized properties, trivial getters, ObjC adapters, bitcode dependencies, and partial-linkage issues. Caches are built only for dependencies, not project modules, because 'a klib residing at some path ... will always stay the same', so up-to-date checks are trivial and no cleanup is needed.
findings.mechanism: CacheStorage.saveAdditionalCacheInfo writes the sidecars. ImportCachesAbiTransformer and ExportCachesAbiVisitor (takeIf isCache) in the lowering list make cached and uncached code agree on accessors and field ABI.

findings.topic: Cache keys are a hand-kept flag string
findings.claim: The cache directory name ('flavor') is built by hand from the options that change machine code: target, -g, -opt, lazy init, sanitizer, stack protector, generic safe casts, latin1 strings, asserts, allocator, gc, gc scheduler, mmap, mark threads, page size, weak sweep, runtime logs, and more. The code comment warns: 'when appending a new flavor into the cache, be sure to update [CompilerConfiguration.setupCommonOptionsForCaches] if needed'.
findings.mechanism: There are two strings: systemCacheFlavorString for stdlib and runtime, and userCacheFlavorString (plus -pl, plus swift_export). Different flavors live in different directories instead of being invalidated. Correctness depends on every new codegen-affecting option being added by hand.

findings.claim: Kotlin 1.9.20 (Experimental, kotlin.incremental.native=true) compiles each Kotlin file to its own .a and stores a file dependency graph. A rebuild recompiles changed files and their dependents. Up-to-date checks look at the file's IR in the klib, not the source text, so they catch changes 'that don't affect the contents of file ... but affect the resolution'.
findings.mechanism: It is built on the same per-file cache machinery as the compiler caches (CacheBuilder.kt). Release builds still cannot use it (F10).

findings.topic: Old memory manager: why it was built
findings.claim: K/N started in 2016 with deferred reference counting, a cycle collector, and thread confinement with 'freezing': an object graph had to be frozen (made immutable) or detached before another thread could see it. The team chose this 'for its simplicity – not because of its memory consumption', and for its closeness to Objective-C ARC.
findings.mechanism: The 2020 roadmap says the RC design makes high allocation throughput hard. Concurrency is the bigger problem: RC systems that work well (Python) restrict threads with a GIL, which was 'not an option' for mobile.

findings.topic: Old memory manager: what broke, and the reversal
findings.claim: Freezing made Kotlin concurrent code hard to share with the JVM. Multithreaded kotlinx.coroutines leaked memory, because the RC algorithm did not track cycles through AtomicReference, and 'we don't have a clear solution'. The team switched to a tracing GC: announced 2020, preview end of summer 2021, default in 1.7.20 (2022), legacy MM removed in 1.9.20 (Nov 2023). Freezing is deprecated and always off.
findings.mechanism: Path: build root-tracking and safepoint infrastructure first, then a simple stop-the-world mark-sweep used 'only for testing' to find forgotten roots, then a concurrent collector. During the transition, compiler caches did not support the legacy MM ('compilation times might worsen'). The change also altered semantics: globals became lazily initialized per file.
findings.numbers: announced Jul 2020; default 1.7.20; removed 1.9.20
sources: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/whatsnew1720.html (section 'The new Kotlin/Native memory manager enabled by default')

findings.topic: New MM: roots via shadow stack, cheap safepoints
findings.claim: K/N finds precise roots with a shadow stack, not stack maps. The function prologue allocates and zeroes a frame of object slots and calls EnterFrame. The epilogue, including exception unwinding, calls LeaveFrame. Safepoints are calls to Kotlin_mm_safePointFunctionPrologue at function entry and Kotlin_mm_safePointWhileLoopBody in loop bodies. The fast path is one load of a global action pointer, with __builtin_expect(action != nullptr, false).
findings.mechanism: The global pointer is set while any SafePointActivator is alive, using a counted mutex. An LLVM pass (RemoveRedundantSafepointsPass) keeps only the first prologue safepoint per basic block or function and inlines it, except on arm32 Apple. Functions marked forbidRuntime get no safepoints. On Apple, the slow path can emit os_signpost intervals for Instruments.

findings.topic: New MM: the default collector today
findings.claim: The default GC is CONCURRENT_MARK_AND_SWEEP. It is non-moving and non-generational, with snapshot-at-the-beginning marking. Steps: stop the world to collect roots; resume mutators with a Dijkstra deletion write barrier into thread-local queues plus a weak-reference read barrier; a marker thread and the mutators build the closure; weak references are processed concurrently; a second short pause disables the barriers. Alternatives are a compile-time choice: pmcs (parallel mark, concurrent sweep), stms (stop-the-world), noop.
findings.mechanism: The GC is chosen per binary ('-Xgc=...'), and the choice is part of the cache key. 1.9.20 added full parallel mark: paused mutators, the GC thread and optional marker threads all drain the mark queue. Before that, a separate GC thread marked global roots and the roots of threads running native code. JetBrains says the old approach did not fit typical iOS apps.
sources: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/whatsnew1920.html (section 'Full parallel mark to reduce the pause time for the GC')

findings.topic: New MM: allocator and pacing numbers
findings.claim: Kotlin 1.9.20 replaced mimalloc with a custom paged allocator. Pages are 256 KiB and are swept on their own, in address order. Each thread owns at most one page per size class. After marking, the GC marks all pages 'needs to be swept before next use' and takes them back from threads. Scheduler defaults: targetHeapBytes 10 MiB, minHeapBytes 5 MiB (20 pages), targetHeapUtilization 0.5 (next target = live / 0.5), trigger at 0.9 × target, timer GC every 10 s (and no later than 2× that).
findings.mechanism: Mutator assists (allocating threads stop and wait for the GC epoch when over target) are on by default only when autoTune is on and maxHeapBytes is unbounded. With a bounded heap, an always-over-target live set would 'look like the program has hanged'. On UIKit, AppStateTracking can turn off the timer GC in the background.
findings.numbers: 256 KiB pages; 10 MiB / 5 MiB / 0.5 / 0.9 / 10 s

findings.topic: ObjC/Swift interop cost under a tracing GC
findings.claim: Swift/ObjC objects that cross into Kotlin are freed only when a GC runs, not promptly as with ARC. A chain Kotlin→Swift→Kotlin→Swift takes one GC cycle per Kotlin hop. A retain cycle with at least one ObjC object can never be reclaimed. deinit runs on the main thread if the object came in on main and the main queue is pumped, and on a special GC thread otherwise. JetBrains advises autoreleasepool around loops that cross the boundary.
findings.mechanism: Kotlin objects held by native code are 'external RC refs'. They are registered in ExternalRCRefRegistry: rc > 0 means the object is in the global roots, and rc == 0 means it 'eventually disappears from roots'. Permanent objects use a special encoding. The count of stable refs in the GC logs is the leak signal.
sources: https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-arc-integration.html (sections Deinitializers, Garbage collection and lifecycle, Support for background state)

findings.topic: Closed world strikes back on iOS
findings.claim: Each Kotlin framework is its own closed world. Two frameworks that both include module :core give Swift two incompatible copies of class Data, so consume(produceData()) does not type-check. The documented fix is one 'umbrella framework' per app. The doc says 'it is never a single library, but a whole world'.
findings.mechanism: This follows from F09: no code sharing between binaries. Binaries can be static, dynamic or a .framework (-Xstatic-framework). C++ and Swift are reached only through C or ObjC headers via cinterop klibs. cinterop klibs carry metadata but no IR.

findings.topic: Two code generators drift (ObjC export to Swift export)
findings.claim: ObjC export (2017) is a set of global batch passes inside the K/N compiler. It has its own LLVM IR generator for the bridges, so 'Kotlin/Native has 2 LLVM IR generators ... Keeping these things in sync requires additional efforts'. It also integrates poorly with the IDE and is tied to K1 descriptors. Swift export (started 2023) is a separate tool: Analysis API → Swift IR → Swift sources plus thin Kotlin bridges with a C header, which the normal K/N compiler builds 'like any other sources'.
findings.mechanism: The bridges became ordinary source for the one compiler. The second codegen path was removed by design.

findings.topic: Kotlin/JS: legacy backend replaced by IR
findings.claim: The old JS compiler produced JS straight from the frontend. It was deprecated when JS IR became Stable in 1.8.0, and in 1.9.0 the LEGACY and BOTH compiler types became errors. Stated reason: 'to unify Kotlin's behavior on all platforms and to make it possible to implement new JS-specific optimizations'. Migration needed code changes 'due to the significant differences between the compilers'. Libraries had to publish IR during the overlap ('joined' legacy+IR klibs).
findings.mechanism: The IR backend gives JS the shared lowerings and whole-program features: production-only DCE (the stdlib is about 1.3 MB as JS, while hello world needs 'a few kilobytes'), member-name minification from class-relation knowledge, lazy top-level property init for startup, per-module incremental caches for development builds, and output granularity per-module (default), per-file or whole-program.
findings.numbers: stdlib about 1.3 MB vs a few KB after DCE (vendor doc)
sources: https://docs.w3cub.com/kotlin~1.9/docs/js-ir-migration (mirror of kotlinlang js-ir-migration for 1.9; rationale paragraph)
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/js-ir-compiler.html (sections Lazy initialization, Incremental compilation, DCE, Minification, output granularity)

findings.topic: Kotlin/Wasm: the host engine owns the GC and the JIT
findings.claim: Kotlin/Wasm maps classes to WasmGC structs, with a vtable struct, a class itable ('<classITable>') and special itable slots for function interfaces. It needs the host's WasmGC and (legacy) exception-handling proposals. All major browsers, Safari included, have supported WasmGC since 11 Dec 2024. Kotlin/Wasm reached Beta in 2.2.20 (Sep 2025). Compose has a 'compatibility mode' that falls back to the JS build on old browsers.
findings.mechanism: There is no Kotlin GC or JIT in the module: the browser engine tiers and collects. The backend is whole-program today (single-module IC fragments plus DCE). JetBrains is working on 'per-module compilation' so changed modules can be rebuilt alone and parts loaded on demand, and the code already has WasmCompilerWithICMultimodule.
sources: https://blog.jetbrains.com/kotlin/2025/09/kotlin-2-2-20-released/ (search result only; not read in full)

findings.topic: HotSpot tiered levels and thresholds (Kotlin/JVM runtime)
findings.claim: HotSpot has five levels: 0 interpreter (profiles into an MDO), 1 C1 without profiling, 2 C1 with invocation and back-edge counters, 3 C1 with full profiling, 4 C2. Defaults: Tier3InvocationThreshold 200, Tier3CompileThreshold 2000, Tier3BackEdgeThreshold 60000 (OSR), Tier4InvocationThreshold 5000, Tier4CompileThreshold 15000, Tier4BackEdgeThreshold 40000. The 0→3 predicate is i > T3Inv*s || (i > T3MinInv*s && i+b > T3Compile*s), where s is a load-feedback scale.
findings.mechanism: Policy depends on compile-queue length. Level 2 is 'about 30% faster' than level 3, so when the C2 queue is long (Tier3DelayOn 5 per compiler thread, off at Tier3DelayOff 2) methods go to level 2 rather than sit at level 3. Tier3LoadFeedback 5 and Tier4LoadFeedback 3 double thresholds as queues grow. Tier0ProfilingStartPercentage 200 starts interpreter profiling when C1 is late. A method can go 0→4 if C1 is too slow.
findings.numbers: 200 / 2000 / 60000 / 5000 / 15000 / 40000; level 3 about 30% slower than level 2

findings.claim: jaotc AOT-compiled classes with Graal into ELF shared libraries (Linux/x64 only at first). Code is checked by class fingerprinting and by the recorded JDK version. Because the code depended on runtime configuration, the JVM looked for four java.base variants by GC × compressed oops (libjava.base.so, -coop, -nong1, -coop-nong1). It had a tiered mode: AOT code did Tier-2-style counting only, and on reaching thresholds was recompiled by C1 at Tier 3 for full profiles, then C2.
findings.mechanism: Non-tiered AOT was 'like statically compiled C++ code': no profiling, no recompilation. It was meant for predictable or no-codegen systems. Compiling java.base needed about 50,000 methods, a 4 GB heap, and an exclusion list of methods that failed to compile.
findings.numbers: 4 variants; about 50,000 methods; -Xmx4g
sources: https://openjdk.org/jeps/295 (Description, 'AOT library modes', 'Steps to generate ... java.base')

findings.claim: JEP 410 removed jaotc, the Graal JIT and HotSpot's src/hotspot/share/aot in JDK 17: 'little use since its introduction and the effort required to maintain it is significant'. The features were left out of Oracle's JDK 16 builds 'and no one complained'. JVMCI was kept.
findings.mechanism: A separate compiler (Graal) and a separate code format (ELF libraries keyed by VM flags) sat beside C1/C2. The replacement (JEP 544) reuses C1/C2 and the CDS-based AOT cache instead.

findings.topic: Leyden JEP 483 (JDK 24): AOT class loading and linking
findings.claim: A training run records, an assembly step creates the cache, and production uses it: -XX:AOTMode=record/create with -XX:AOTConfiguration and -XX:AOTCache. It cut startup by 42% on HelloStream (0.031→0.018 s, 11.4 MB cache) and on Spring PetClinic 3.2.0 (about 21,000 classes, 4.486→2.604 s, 130 MB cache). Most of PetClinic's gain came from the CDS part, which already existed.
findings.mechanism: Validity rules: same JDK release, OS and architecture; the class path must match or only append; module options must be identical; no class-rewriting JVMTI agents. On a mismatch the default is to warn and ignore the cache. AOTMode=on, renamed AOTMode=required in JDK 27, makes a mismatch fatal. The GC and the main class may differ. Classes from user-defined loaders and signed classes fall back to JIT-time loading. The cache format is 'not specified and is subject to change without notice'.
sources: https://openjdk.org/jeps/483 (Description, Consistency of training and subsequent runs, Future work)

findings.claim: JEP 514 adds a one-step -XX:AOTCacheOutput: the launcher runs record then create as sub-invocations, uses a temporary configuration file, and takes JDK_AOT_VM_OPTIONS for the create step only. JEP 515 stores method profiles in the cache. A Stream-API program went from 90 to 73 ms (19%) for 250 KB more (+2.5%). 'Profiles cached during training runs do not prevent additional profiling during production runs'.
findings.mechanism: Cached profiles let C2 start right away, and on-line profiling keeps running, so production behavior can override training behavior. JEP 515 states the end goal: 'A partial AOT solution, where reasonable AOT code is gradually replaced by better-optimized JIT code'.

findings.topic: Leyden JEP 544 (JDK 28): AOT code that keeps the JIT
findings.claim: JEP 544 (status Completed, Release 28, page updated 2026-11-11) stores C1/C2 native code from the training run in the AOT cache. AOT and JIT code coexist and are 'completely interoperable since they are created by the same compilers'. On a 2-core Linux/x64 box, the cache alone cut startup about 50-70% across five framework apps, and with AOT code about 65-80%. On a javac loop: about 30% from the cache, plus about 45% from AOT code, about 75% total. Near steady state by iteration 4.
findings.mechanism: Extra validity rules: same CPU architecture AND the same CPU features (AVX-512 code will not run without it), and the same GC, 'since AOT code contains GC-specific read/write barriers'. If these fail, only the AOT code is dropped; classes and profiles in the cache are still used. 'It is not a goal to provide an AOT-only mode'. Future work found that minimizing the interpreter 'results in overly large AOT cache files, which can take more time to load than just running the interpreter', and minimizing the JIT 'often leads to lower peak performance'. -XX:-AOTCodeCaching turns it off; 'cached code can make the AOT cache significantly larger'.
sources: https://openjdk.org/jeps/544 (Summary, Non-Goals, Motivation 'What about static compilation?', Description, Consistency, Future Work)

findings.claim: JEP 544 lists three advantages of dynamic over static compilation: it adapts to changed hot spots by deopt and reopt, it is portable across CPU, OS and JDK, and it handles dynamic loading, linkage and reflection. It says static compilers resort to 'closed-world assumptions' and to making developers 'identify in advance the classes eligible for reflection'. It also concedes that static code 'can even be competitive with HotSpot if ... guided by accurate profiles'.
findings.mechanism: This is the JVM team's design position against the Kotlin/Native and GraalVM native-image model. Both teams agree that a closed world buys whole-program optimization at the cost of dynamism.

findings.topic: Debug vs release split on Native
findings.claim: In K/N, debug and release are different products, not one pipeline with different knobs. Debug uses compiler caches and per-file incremental builds, LLVM at NONE or DEFAULT, and the runtime linked 'Optimize'. Release runs the global optimizations, LLVM AGGRESSIVE (Oz with smallBinary), full LTO over one module, and no caches. JetBrains' compile-time advice is to build only linkDebug* during development, and only for the platform in use.
findings.mechanism: createLTOFinalPipelineConfig picks the level from shouldOptimize/shouldContainDebugInfo. runtimeLinkageStrategy defaults to Optimize in debug only, 'intentionally'.

findings.topic: Pre-codegen inliner and its ordering conflicts
findings.claim: K/N has an optional pre-codegen IR inliner (BinaryOptions.preCodegenInlineThreshold, default 0 = off). It runs only with global optimizations. Its comments record a conflict between passes: removing redundant static-initializer calls 'is more optimal but contradicts with the pre-codegen inliner' (KT-72336), and the inliner 'is not entirely correct since coroutinesLivenessAnalysisPhase could be turned off'.
findings.mechanism: Which passes are enabled changes which other passes are correct. The phase list encodes this with disable = enablePreCodegenInliner || !runGlobalOptimizations.

lessons.lesson: Copy FIR's phase contract into the ep9 front end. Use a fixed ordered list of resolve phases, with the rule 'what phase B sees is resolved to every earlier phase'. Store early errors in the tree and report them in one final check phase. Then batch compile (AOT unit build) and lazy compile (H04) are the same code run in a different order, and they cannot report different early errors.

Keep one shared IR and one ordered, named pass list per mode (jit, jitless, hybrid). Do not build separate compilers. Give each pass a dumper and a validator, and add stage-boundary validators with stage-specific invariants (Kotlin: 'no inline call sites remain', 'unbound symbols allowed here'). Treat a pass that is only sound when another pass is off (Kotlin KT-72336) as a bug to fix, not a flag to keep. This matches doc 13 §2.2 'one optimizer, three branches'.

Do not derive the AOT unit's compatibility key from a hand-written list. Kotlin's cache flavor string has a 'be sure to update' comment, so one missed option means wrong cached code. In ep9, generate the H35 header version fields and the code-cache key from one registry of codegen-affecting options (GC barriers, CPU features, layout versions, TS flags), and add a test that fails when a new ExecOptions or build flag is missing from the key.

Make mismatch handling fine-grained, the way Kotlin partial linkage and Leyden do. Kotlin turns a broken reference into a throwing stub for that declaration only. Leyden drops only the AOT code on a CPU or GC mismatch and keeps the classes and profiles. ep9's 'identity ladder: drop the smallest thing that fails' (doc 13 §5.1) is the right shape. Extend it to per-function drops (one function's AOT code to bytecode) and keep the facts and bytecode sections when only the text section is bad. Never fail the whole load when a smaller drop works.

Decide and write down what happens when unit A inlines code from unit B and B changes. Kotlin froze inlined bodies (JVM model) because inline is a language contract. JS has no such contract, since module bindings are live, so ep9 cannot freeze. It must record B's digest and drop A's optimized code on a mismatch. That is what H35 container v2 kind 10 'deps' does. Keep it mandatory and add tests for 'dependency changed, inliner stale'.

A closed-world proof can replace a guard only if nothing outside can break it. Kotlin/Native skips the last type check and turns an empty callee set into a throw. That is safe only because the whole binary is known, and it is lost as soon as separately compiled caches exist. In JS, any unit or eval can add a class or patch a prototype. So in ep9 every devirtualized call in an AOT unit needs a guard or a fuse plus a fallback path.
